name: Monitoring Tier Adjustment
consequences: Increasing the frequency of enhanced PSG nights improves physiological resolution but raises participant burden and operational complexity. Reduced sensor deployment lowers data richness but eases technical maintenance, potentially missing rare events critical for phenotyping.
options: Implement enhanced PSG on all nights for high-risk participants with infrequent events
Replace contact-free mattress sensors with periodic manual checks to reduce false positives
Integrate real-time anomaly detection algorithms to trigger ad-hoc PSG escalation
review: Prioritizing data depth over participant comfort risks compliance attrition, while sensor reduction leaves gaps in baseline physiological characterization.

name: Staffing Ratio Optimization
consequences: Adding night technicians improves response times to emergencies but increases labor costs. Reducing shifts per technician risks fatigue-induced errors during critical event capture.
options: Hire part-time clinical psychologists for overnight behavioral intervention support
Implement staggered shift handoffs with mandatory 2-hour overlap during high-risk periods
Train bed partners as secondary monitors for low-risk participants
review: Cost control measures may compromise safety margins, while expanded staffing leaves unaddressed risks of over-reliance on human judgment during technical failures.

name: Recruitment Criterion Refinement
consequences: Broadening inclusion criteria increases participant diversity but introduces confounding variables from comorbid conditions. Strict exclusions ensure clinical homogeneity but limit generalizability of event patterns.
options: Prioritize recruitment from regions with higher parasomnia prevalence through regional sleep clinic partnerships
Institute a tiered eligibility system based on self-reported episode frequency and collateral history reliability
Offer extended stay incentives to participants with zero captured events to improve data yield
review: Expanding access risks diluting clinical focus, while retention strategies may create unintended selection bias in event frequency metrics.

name: Data Sharing Protocol
consequences: Expanding de-identified data deposition accelerates external validation but increases privacy breach risks. Restricting sharing limits collaborative analysis opportunities and reproducibility.
options: Create a controlled-access portal with dynamic data release based on participant consent tiers
Implement synthetic data generation for non-physiological sensor streams while retaining real EEG data
Establish a data use agreement framework with academic partners for joint publication opportunities
review: Balancing openness with privacy constraints leaves unresolved challenges in handling incidental findings from unstructured sensor data.

name: Facility Expansion Timing
consequences: Accelerating to 12 suites enables higher throughput but strains maintenance resources and increases space utilization risks. Delaying expansion preserves financial flexibility but limits capacity during peak recruitment periods.
options: Convert adjacent residential units into temporary suites during high-demand enrollment phases
Implement a reservation system for suite usage based on participant event frequency projections
Outsource non-critical maintenance to local contractors during off-peak hours
review: Capacity scaling decisions create tension between operational agility and long-term infrastructure planning, leaving unaddressed risks of overextension during unexpected demand spikes.

name: Technology Integration Strategy
consequences: Adopting next-generation EEG headbands improves signal quality but requires revalidation of existing annotation workflows. Retaining legacy systems ensures continuity but limits methodological innovation.
options: Pilot hybrid sensor arrays combining dry-electrode EEG with inertial measurement units for movement tracking
Develop custom firmware to enable real-time artifact detection and automatic signal rejection
Partner with sensor manufacturers for co-development of parasomnia-specific monitoring protocols
review: Innovation investments risk disrupting established workflows, while conservative tech choices may hinder competitive differentiation in event-triage algorithm development.

name: Community Engagement Model
consequences: Establishing local partnerships increases recruitment efficiency but requires ongoing relationship management. Relying on academic networks limits reach to underrepresented populations.
options: Create a patient advisory board with parasomnia advocates to co-design recruitment materials and consent processes
Launch a public education campaign highlighting the facility's role in advancing sleep medicine through social media and local media outlets
Develop a referral incentive program for healthcare providers with high parasomnia patient volumes
review: Community-focused strategies may dilute clinical focus, while provider incentives create unaddressed risks of over-reliance on specific referral sources.

name: Participant Retention Framework
consequences: Implementing tiered incentive structures for prolonged stays increases enrollment stability but risks dependency on financial compensation as the primary motivator. This could distort participant demographics or create expectations of indefinite support beyond the study's scope.
options: Offer incremental compensation boosts for participants who complete 80% of scheduled nights
Establish a peer mentorship program pairing long-stay participants with new enrollees to foster community bonds
Integrate participant feedback into protocol design through quarterly advisory panels
review: Prioritizing financial incentives over intrinsic motivation risks creating a transactional participant culture, while the absence of non-monetary engagement strategies leaves psychological retention unaddressed.

name: Safety Protocol Calibration
consequences: Adjusting sensor sensitivity thresholds to reduce false alarms improves technician efficiency but may miss subtle behavioral cues critical for rare parasomnia events, creating a trade-off between operational throughput and data completeness.
options: Implement dynamic threshold adjustments based on participant-specific baseline metrics
Deploy secondary verification protocols for ambiguous sensor triggers involving bed partner audio logs
Schedule monthly safety protocol audits with external sleep medicine experts
review: Optimizing for false negative reduction creates a blind spot for atypical event patterns, while the lack of real-time calibration tools limits adaptability during active monitoring.

name: Data Analysis Methodology
consequences: Adopting machine learning-based pattern recognition accelerates annotation throughput but introduces interpretability challenges that could undermine AASM criterion adherence, requiring additional validation layers to maintain clinical credibility.
options: Develop hybrid models combining algorithmic flagging with human-in-the-loop verification for ambiguous cases
Create standardized benchmark datasets from pilot phase data to train and test analytical tools
Implement cross-validation across multiple independent scoring teams for algorithmic outputs
review: Algorithmic augmentation risks obscuring clinical context, while the absence of a clear validation hierarchy leaves methodological consistency vulnerable to scorer bias.

name: Collaborative Research Partnerships
consequences: Forming alliances with regional sleep clinics expands recruitment reach but may create dependency on external referral networks, potentially limiting the facility's ability to independently define inclusion criteria.
options: Establish joint protocol development committees with partner clinics to align inclusion/exclusion standards
Create a shared data repository for anonymized clinical cases to inform recruitment strategies
Develop reciprocal training programs for clinic staff on the facility's monitoring protocols
review: External collaboration risks diluting methodological control, while the lack of formalized knowledge transfer mechanisms could hinder long-term operational independence.

name: Funding Diversification Strategy
consequences: Pursuing industry partnerships introduces potential conflicts of interest but provides additional resources for infrastructure upgrades, requiring strict separation protocols to maintain academic integrity.
options: Structure industry collaborations around specific technical support needs rather than research direction
Implement transparent conflict-of-interest disclosure processes for all partnership agreements
Reserve 20% of industry funds for independent third-party audit of research outcomes
review: Financial dependencies create vulnerability to external priorities, while the absence of clear governance boundaries leaves ethical oversight incomplete.

name: Regulatory Compliance Streamlining
consequences: Standardizing documentation workflows for ethics approvals accelerates protocol implementation but may reduce flexibility to adapt to unforeseen regulatory requirements during the study's lifecycle.
options: Create modular compliance templates adaptable to different regulatory jurisdictions
Establish a dedicated regulatory liaison role for continuous oversight
Implement automated compliance checklists integrated with project management software
review: Process optimization creates rigidity in regulatory responses, while the lack of scenario-based contingency planning leaves unexpected requirements unaddressed.

name: Environmental Control Optimization
consequences: Fine-tuning ambient conditions to minimize sleep disruption improves data quality but increases operational complexity through continuous monitoring and adjustment requirements.
options: Implement adaptive climate control systems responding to real-time sleep stage data
Create standardized environmental baseline metrics for all sleep suites
Schedule weekly environmental audits with sleep physiology experts
review: Micro-managing environmental factors creates maintenance burdens, while the absence of a failure mode analysis leaves unexpected disruptions unmitigated.

name: Residential Safety Configuration
consequences: Adjusting physical safety measures alters risk exposure profiles and maintenance overhead. Over-securing the environment risks compromising naturalistic behavior capture, while under-securing increases liability and potential participant harm during unmonitored episodes.
options: Implementing real-time biometric access controls for corridor entry
Redesigning corridor layouts to minimize fall risks during nocturnal episodes
Introducing automated emergency response systems with voice-activated alert triggers
review: Enhanced safety measures increase operational complexity and maintenance costs, leaving unaddressed the trade-off between behavioral authenticity and injury prevention in unobserved nocturnal scenarios.

name: Data Annotation Workflow
consequences: Changing annotation procedures affects inter-rater reliability and data throughput. Centralizing annotation risks bottlenecking analysis, while decentralizing it introduces variability that undermines methodological consistency.
options: Establishing a tiered annotation system with initial technician review followed by senior rater validation
Implementing double-blind annotation rounds with randomized participant masking
Developing a semi-automated pre-screening tool to flag ambiguous events for human review
review: Centralized annotation improves consistency but creates capacity constraints, leaving unaddressed the challenge of maintaining high throughput without compromising inter-rater agreement.

name: Control Group Integration
consequences: Modifying control group composition alters benchmarking validity. Expanding inclusion criteria risks diluting baseline metrics, while strict criteria may limit statistical power and generalizability.
options: Matching control participants to parasomnia cohort on sleep architecture metrics and demographic factors
Implementing a staggered control group enrollment to maintain temporal comparability
Using historical data from previous sleep studies as a reference cohort
review: Strict control group matching increases recruitment burden, leaving unaddressed the risk of overfitting analytical models to specific demographic subgroups.

name: Staffing Shift Rotation
consequences: Altering shift patterns affects both staff well-being and data continuity. Extended shifts risk fatigue-related errors, while frequent rotations disrupt institutional knowledge retention.
options: Implementing 12-hour shift blocks with mandatory 8-hour recovery periods between shifts
Creating cross-training protocols to enable staff flexibility across monitoring and annotation roles
Introducing staggered shift start times to maintain 24/7 coverage with reduced staff numbers
review: Extended shifts increase fatigue risk, leaving unaddressed the challenge of maintaining consistent data quality during high-stress operational periods.

name: Sensor Calibration Protocol
consequences: Revising calibration schedules impacts data reliability and equipment maintenance costs. Frequent calibration ensures precision but increases operational downtime, while infrequent calibration risks data drift.
options: Implementing automated daily calibration routines with real-time error detection
Establishing a biweekly manual calibration schedule with technician verification
Using environmental sensors to trigger adaptive calibration based on ambient conditions
review: Automated calibration increases technical complexity, leaving unaddressed the risk of over-reliance on algorithmic corrections without human oversight.

name: Participant Onboarding Process
consequences: Modifying enrollment procedures affects recruitment efficiency and participant readiness. Streamlined onboarding risks incomplete consent understanding, while exhaustive processes may deter participation.
options: Creating a multi-stage consent process with interactive multimedia explanations
Implementing a pre-admission virtual tour of the facility with safety protocol walkthroughs
Establishing a peer mentorship program for new participants to share experiences
review: Interactive onboarding increases engagement but creates dependency on technical infrastructure, leaving unaddressed the challenge of supporting participants with limited digital literacy.

name: Regulatory Adherence Verification
consequences: Changing compliance verification methods affects audit readiness and administrative burden. Formalized audits ensure documentation rigor but slow operational agility, while informal checks risk regulatory noncompliance.
options: Implementing a real-time regulatory compliance dashboard with automated audit trail generation
Creating a dedicated compliance officer role with direct PI reporting access
Establishing quarterly third-party audit reviews with institutional oversight
review: Formalized audits increase administrative workload, leaving unaddressed the risk of bureaucratic delays during critical operational phases.
